These are feedback notes, not a script students must reproduce. Keep this file outside the student distribution. Numerical results are calculated from the prepared datasets when rendered. Accept alternative explanations when the statistical question and limitations are clear.

small <- read.csv("data/mmse_small.csv")
control <- small$MMSE[small$Group == "Control"]
ad <- small$MMSE[small$Group == "AD"]
mmse <- read.csv("data/mmse_baseline.csv")
neurites <- read.csv("data/neurites.csv")
describe <- function(x) {
  c(n = sum(!is.na(x)), mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE), SD = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q1 = unname(quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)),
    Q3 = unname(quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)), IQR = IQR(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}

Notebook 1

Exercise 1: the original vector’s mean is 28.5; adding 26 gives 28. Assignment stores the four values under a name. Scores and scores are distinct objects.

Exercise 2: 20 rows, 3 columns. Teaching_ID identifies a row, Group is nominal, MMSE is a bounded discrete score. Equal vector lengths do not establish pairing. A score difference is useful descriptively but does not imply a calibrated equal change in overall cognition at every part of the scale.

Exercises 3–4: ten scores in each group. Group selection should agree with table(small$Group).

knitr::kable(rbind(Control = describe(control), AD = describe(ad)), digits = 3)
n mean median SD Q1 Q3 IQR
Control 10 28.1 28.0 1.197 27.00 28.75 1.75
AD 10 9.0 9.5 2.449 7.25 10.75 3.50

The AD group has greater observed spread. A mean alone hides that difference. These synthetic values support practice, not conclusions about actual patients.

The separate assay example changes the mean from 5.4 to 10 while leaving the median at 5. Investigate an extreme observation’s source; do not remove it just to improve a p-value. Patient IDs have no meaningful average; ordinal SES codes do not establish equal intervals.

Exercise 5: three observed scores give a mean of 85/3 = 28.333. Replacing the missing value by zero gives 21.25, a different and unjustified calculation. Missingness should be counted and considered scientifically.

Notebook 2

The control histogram is concentrated near the upper score limit; AD scores are more spread and lower. Four-point bins conceal some integer detail without changing the observations. Neither a bell-like histogram nor a mean close to a median proves normality.

Boxplots show medians and hinges, not confidence intervals. Jitter is horizontal only; points preserve their score values. Mean bars conceal spread, sample size, and repeated values. A violin estimates a smooth density: with ten observations and tied scores, that smoothness can overstate how much is known about shape. Its width is not uncertainty. A caption should name MMSE points, the two groups, and ten observations each.

Notebook 3

Question and distributions

The initial target is the population mean-score difference under the independent-person teaching assumption, estimated by AD minus control. This is not a treatment experiment. A paired method would require matched observations, not equal counts.

shapiro.test(control)
##
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
##
## data:  control
## W = 0.82361, p-value = 0.02802
shapiro.test(ad)
##
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
##
## data:  ad
## W = 0.94219, p-value = 0.5776

A suitable correction to the student’s sentence is: “The Shapiro–Wilk test did not detect sufficient evidence against normality. This does not prove that the data are normally distributed, particularly with a small sample. Before using a t-test, we should also inspect each group’s plots, consider sample size and extreme values, and check that the observations are independent.” The analysis must also address the intended question about means.

Discuss the actual plots even if Shapiro does not reject at 0.05. The control values are discrete and constrained by a ceiling. Ten observations cannot provide strong reassurance about tails. Pooling the strongly separated groups answers the wrong normality question for this comparison.

Mean and rank comparisons

mean(ad) - mean(control)
## [1] -19.1
t.test(ad, control)
##
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
##
## data:  ad and control
## t = -22.153, df = 13.068, p-value = 9.486e-12
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -20.96162 -17.23838
## sample estimates:
## mean of x mean of y
##       9.0      28.1
wilcox.test(ad, control, exact = FALSE)
##
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
##
## data:  ad and control
## W = 0, p-value = 0.0001659
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

The observed mean difference is −19.1 points. The CI is for AD minus control, not for individual scores. A small p-value neither measures the probability the null hypothesis is true nor proves clinical importance or valid assumptions. Failure to reject is not equivalence.

Wilcoxon addresses rank ordering under its framework, not equality of means and not generally equality of medians without shape assumptions. Both methods require independent participants. A good answer identifies the target, acknowledges bounds/ties and small-sample approximation limits, and explains why a chosen primary method fits the question. Do not grade on whether students choose the instructor’s preferred method alone.

Both analyses here provide strong evidence for their respective questions. Agreement does not prove normality. If asked about disagreement, students should revisit shapes, influential values, assumptions, and the target, rather than selecting the smaller p-value. The rank-sum W and Shapiro W have different meanings.

Overlap example

mean(neurites$condition_1) - mean(neurites$control)
## [1] 0.430004
t.test(neurites$condition_1, neurites$control)
##
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
##
## data:  neurites$condition_1 and neurites$control
## t = 5.5659, df = 36.835, p-value = 2.465e-06
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.2734427 0.5865654
## sample estimates:
## mean of x mean of y
## 0.9314173 0.5014132

The mean difference is about 0.430 recorded units, CI about 0.273–0.587. Individual ranges overlap but the uncertainty interval for a mean difference excludes zero. These are different quantities. The synthetic data’s physical units and generation design are undocumented; independent observations are an explicit teaching assumption.

Correlation demonstration

cor.test(mmse$Age, mmse$MMSE, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
##
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
##
## data:  mmse$Age and mmse$MMSE
## S = 477342, p-value = 0.1075
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##        rho
## -0.1386425

Report rho and n = 136. The association is cross-sectional and cannot establish within-person cognitive decline with ageing. Discuss ceiling effects and group composition. Spearman’s approximate p-value handles ties explicitly; no Spearman CI is supplied by base R.

Notebook 4

Worked correction and data audit

p <- c(A = 0.01, B = 0.03, C = 0.20)
data.frame(raw = p, adjusted = p.adjust(p, "bonferroni"))
##    raw adjusted
## A 0.01     0.03
## B 0.03     0.09
## C 0.20     0.60

All three prespecified comparisons form the example’s family. A and B fall below 0.05 before adjustment; only A does after it. Adjustment changes the evidence criterion, not the observed treatment differences. Selective reporting would conceal the number of tests tried.

dim(mmse)
## [1] 136  13
length(unique(mmse$Subject_ID))
## [1] 136
table(mmse$Group)
##
##    Demented Nondemented
##          64          72
colSums(is.na(mmse))
## Source_row Subject_ID      Visit      Group        M.F        Age       EDUC
##          0          0          0          0          0          0          0
##        SES       MMSE        CDR       eTIV       nWBV        ASF
##          8          0          0          0          0          0
range(mmse$Age)
## [1] 60 96
range(mmse$MMSE)
## [1] 17 30

There are 136 independent participants in 13 columns, 72 Nondemented and 64 Demented; eight SES values are missing. No MMSE values are missing in this selected baseline dataset. This differs from the old visit-level file; do not use its old counts in feedback.

The IDs and Visit == 1 selection address repeated observations. This does not remove selection bias, measurement limitations, or confounding. The exclusion of the Converted group preserves the earlier course selection and depends on longitudinal information.

Group comparison reference

non <- mmse$MMSE[mmse$Group == "Nondemented"]
dem <- mmse$MMSE[mmse$Group == "Demented"]
knitr::kable(rbind(Nondemented = describe(non), Demented = describe(dem)), digits = 3)
n mean median SD Q1 Q3 IQR
Nondemented 72 29.194 29 0.850 29 30 1
Demented 64 25.328 26 3.319 23 28 5 
shapiro.test(non)
##
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
##
## data:  non
## W = 0.79825, p-value = 1.54e-08
shapiro.test(dem)
##
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
##
## data:  dem
## W = 0.94879, p-value = 0.009978
t.test(dem, non)
##
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
##
## data:  dem and non
## t = -9.0583, df = 70.344, p-value = 1.983e-13
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -4.717525 -3.015114
## sample estimates:
## mean of x mean of y
##  25.32812  29.19444
wilcox.test(dem, non, exact = FALSE)
##
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
##
## data:  dem and non
## W = 632, p-value = 9.963e-14
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

The reference includes both methods for marking, although students choose one primary comparison. The score distributions have different shapes and a ceiling, especially in the Nondemented group. A Wilcoxon result should not be reported as a test of a median difference without additional assumptions. A Welch analysis answers the mean question but needs a discussion of its approximate inference on bounded distributions. Expect direction, relevant summaries, sample sizes, test statistic and p-value, and a confidence interval when using Welch.

Do not accept “Shapiro was significant, therefore Wilcoxon” as a complete justification. Ask what question the rank comparison answers. Do not accept “large n means assumptions no longer matter” either.

Correlation reference: students choose only one

point_colours <- ifelse(mmse$Group == "Demented", "#B34D22", "#246B91")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(mmse$Age, mmse$MMSE, pch = 16, col = point_colours,
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "MMSE score (points)")
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Demented", "Nondemented"),
       col = c("#B34D22", "#246B91"), pch = 16, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
plot(mmse$nWBV, mmse$MMSE, pch = 16, col = point_colours,
     xlab = "nWBV (fraction)", ylab = "MMSE score (points)")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
for (variable in c("Age", "nWBV")) {
  for (method in c("pearson", "spearman")) {
    cat("\n", variable, "and MMSE:", method, "\n")
    result <- cor.test(mmse[[variable]], mmse$MMSE, method = method, exact = FALSE)
    print(result)
  }
}
##
##  Age and MMSE: pearson
##
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
##
## data:  mmse[[variable]] and mmse$MMSE
## t = -0.42326, df = 134, p-value = 0.6728
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.2036201  0.1326089
## sample estimates:
##         cor
## -0.03653964
##
##
##  Age and MMSE: spearman
##
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
##
## data:  mmse[[variable]] and mmse$MMSE
## S = 477342, p-value = 0.1075
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##        rho
## -0.1386425
##
##
##  nWBV and MMSE: pearson
##
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
##
## data:  mmse[[variable]] and mmse$MMSE
## t = 4.1945, df = 134, p-value = 4.942e-05
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.1828284 0.4814025
## sample estimates:
##       cor
## 0.3406766
##
##
##  nWBV and MMSE: spearman
##
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
##
## data:  mmse[[variable]] and mmse$MMSE
## S = 282575, p-value = 0.0001078
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##       rho
## 0.3259501

All options have 136 complete pairs. Award credit for choosing a linear or monotonic question and inspecting the plot, not for obtaining a particular coefficient. Pearson’s usual inference has assumptions; Spearman does not answer every nonlinear question and does not come with a base-R CI.

Colouring the scatterplot by group can reveal that between-group separation contributes to the pooled association. It does not itself adjust for group or establish causality. The student need only investigate one limitation, not run more subgroup tests.

Minimum submission feedback

Check for actual selected-test outputs; the blank template intentionally renders without doing inferential tests. Required work is one primary comparison, one correlation, and the separate correction explanation. If a student leaves selection messages, empty answer prompts, or only a screenshot of a result, ask them to complete the reasoning and code.

Good work connects the question, observation unit, assumptions, result and limitation. Allow short, direct answers. Partners may share code, but each should explain it. Ask each student to interpret one figure or predict the effect of changing an argument. LLM use itself is neither rewarded nor penalised; understanding and verification matter.

An overall discovery claim based on either of the two analyses needs multiplicity considered. Students can acknowledge the exploratory, unadjusted scope; an optional supplied two-test adjustment is available. Never encourage additional testing to find significance.

Additional practice: worked answers

Notebook 1: neurite import, selection, summaries, and calibration

head(neurites)
##      control condition_1 condition_2
## 1 0.06372999   0.7305269    1.097290
## 2 0.10308265   1.1828578    3.920390
## 3 0.99902660   0.7414197    5.523907
## 4 0.60876101   0.6742225    7.151884
## 5 0.63159041   1.0256576    7.167801
## 6 0.39914599   1.4141315    7.611765
dim(neurites)
## [1] 20  3
names(neurites)
## [1] "control"     "condition_1" "condition_2"
str(neurites)
## 'data.frame':    20 obs. of  3 variables:
##  $ control    : num  0.0637 0.1031 0.999 0.6088 0.6316 ...
##  $ condition_1: num  0.731 1.183 0.741 0.674 1.026 ...
##  $ condition_2: num  1.1 3.92 5.52 7.15 7.17 ...
neurites$condition_2[neurites$condition_2 > 5]
## [1]  5.523907  7.151884  7.167801  7.611765  6.451793 11.107930  5.811697
sum(neurites$condition_2 > 5)
## [1] 7
knitr::kable(t(vapply(neurites, describe, numeric(7))), digits = 3)
n mean median SD Q1 Q3 IQR
control 20 0.501 0.490 0.265 0.363 0.676 0.313
condition_1 20 0.931 0.921 0.222 0.834 1.040 0.206
condition_2 20 3.724 3.246 3.125 1.074 5.972 4.898 
lengths_um <- c(12.3, 15.8, 9.4, 18.1)
calibrated_um <- lengths_um * 0.98 - 0.15
calibrated_um
## [1] 11.904 15.334  9.062 17.588
calibrated_um[calibrated_um > 15]
## [1] 15.334 17.588
which(calibrated_um > 15)
## [1] 2 4

The wide neurite table has twenty rows and three condition columns: sixty measurements under the independent-culture teaching assumption. Condition 2 has both the largest mean and SD. A row does not define matched cultures. Calibration decreases each of the positive example lengths; positions 2 and 4 remain above 15 µm.

Notebook 2: histogram and table-format practice

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(neurites$control, breaks = 5, main = "Control", xlab = "Recorded units")
hist(neurites$condition_1, breaks = 5, main = "Condition 1", xlab = "Recorded units")
hist(neurites$condition_2, breaks = 5, main = "Condition 2: breaks = 5", xlab = "Recorded units")
hist(neurites$condition_2, breaks = 15, main = "Condition 2: breaks = 15", xlab = "Recorded units")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The numeric breaks argument is a suggestion; explicit boundaries set exact bins. The condition 2 range exceeds 1.6, so the control/condition 1 boundaries cannot contain its values. Very fine bins are sparse with twenty observations. A shared 0–12 horizontal scale preserves comparability but compresses the narrow groups. Neither bin choice changes the original measurements. Do not grade a particular number of apparent peaks as a population fact.

boxplot(neurites, outline = FALSE, main = "Three synthetic conditions",
        ylab = "Neurite measurement (recorded units)")
set.seed(7)
stripchart(neurites, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter", add = TRUE, pch = 16)

neurites_long <- stack(neurites)
names(neurites_long) <- c("measurement", "condition")
dim(neurites_long)
## [1] 60  2
head(neurites_long[neurites_long$condition == "condition_2", ])
##    measurement   condition
## 41    1.097290 condition_2
## 42    3.920390 condition_2
## 43    5.523907 condition_2
## 44    7.151884 condition_2
## 45    7.167801 condition_2
## 46    7.611765 condition_2

The long table has sixty rows and two columns. Reshaping changes the arrangement, not the number of measurements. The broad condition 2 also compresses the first two boxes; a separate control/condition 1 plot is useful for their overlap. Check exported PDFs for readable labels and that dev.off() was run.

Notebook 3: neurite diagnostics and comparison

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (condition in names(neurites)) {
  qqnorm(neurites[[condition]], main = condition)
  qqline(neurites[[condition]])
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
normality_p <- vapply(neurites, function(x) shapiro.test(x)$p.value, numeric(1))
normality_p
##     control condition_1 condition_2
##   0.7651610   0.9378696   0.1111495
wilcox.test(neurites$condition_1, neurites$control, exact = FALSE)
##
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
##
## data:  neurites$condition_1 and neurites$control
## W = 358, p-value = 2.041e-05
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
shapiro.test(unlist(neurites, use.names = FALSE))
##
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
##
## data:  unlist(neurites, use.names = FALSE)
## W = 0.64966, p-value = 1.066e-10

Read the plotted departures alongside the p-values, including any ambiguous cases. Different spread alone is not non-normality. Condition 2 is much more variable and has an uneven sample shape; avoid claiming that either rejection or non-rejection settles its population distribution. Pooling combines different centres and spreads, so its normality assessment addresses a different distribution.

nt1 <- t.test(neurites$condition_1, neurites$control)
nt2 <- t.test(neurites$condition_2, neurites$control)
np <- c(condition_1 = nt1$p.value, condition_2 = nt2$p.value)
data.frame(mean_difference = c(mean(neurites$condition_1) - mean(neurites$control),
                               mean(neurites$condition_2) - mean(neurites$control)),
           raw_p = np, bonferroni_p = p.adjust(np, "bonferroni"))
##             mean_difference        raw_p bonferroni_p
## condition_1        0.430004 2.464903e-06 4.929806e-06
## condition_2        3.222831 1.911231e-04 3.822462e-04

Condition 2 has the larger mean difference but greater variability. Students should read the actual p-values and connect their ordering to uncertainty rather than equate a larger effect with stronger evidence. The two comparisons form the declared family; adjustment does not change the effects. Reversing AD minus control changes the sign of the mean difference and reverses the confidence-interval endpoints’ signs, not the two-sided evidence.

Notebook 4: descriptive overview and four-panel figure

describe(mmse$Age)
##          n       mean     median         SD         Q1         Q3        IQR
## 136.000000  75.279412  75.000000   7.539222  70.000000  80.000000  10.000000
range(mmse$Age)
## [1] 60 96
table(mmse$M.F)
##
##  F  M
## 78 58
table(mmse$SES, useNA = "ifany")
##
##    1    2    3    4    5 <NA>
##   26   39   31   29    3    8
older <- mmse[mmse$Age >= 80, ]
nrow(older)
## [1] 39
table(older$Group)
##
##    Demented Nondemented
##          17          22
nrow(older) / nrow(mmse)
## [1] 0.2867647

Category bars count distinct labels; a histogram bins a numeric measurement scale. SES is ordinal, with eight missing values and no legitimate category zero. The age threshold does not define disease or justify an extra hypothesis test. Summaries describe this selected sample, not all dementia patients.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(mmse$Age, breaks = 8, main = "Participant ages", xlab = "Age (years)")
boxplot(MMSE ~ Group, data = mmse, main = "MMSE by group", ylab = "MMSE score (points)")
plot(mmse$Age, mmse$MMSE, pch = 16, main = "Age and MMSE",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "MMSE score (points)")
ses_counts <- table(mmse$SES, useNA = "ifany")
ses_labels <- names(ses_counts)
ses_labels[is.na(ses_labels)] <- "Missing"
barplot(ses_counts, names.arg = ses_labels, main = "SES including missing values",
        xlab = "SES category", ylab = "Participants")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Accept the chosen nWBV scatterplot instead of age. Every panel needs its scale and meaning. A combined figure is a communication exercise, not a reason to add tests. For the further measurement exercise, EDUC is years of education and nWBV a fraction; accept a descriptive question and explicit limits to interpretation.
